The thyristors are numbered in firing order T1 … T6, fired every 60°; each conducts for 120°, one from the top group and one from the bottom group at a time.</figcaption></figure>

**How it works**

- The three-phase supply ($V_a$, $V_b$, $V_c$) feeds six thyristors, T1 to T6.
- At any time **one upper and one lower thyristor** conduct, connecting the phase with the highest voltage to the positive DC terminal and the phase with the lowest voltage to the negative terminal.
- The thyristors are fired in sequence **every 60°**, giving a fairly smooth DC output with six pulses per cycle. **Each thyristor conducts for 120°.**
- Changing the firing angle $\alpha$ controls the average DC output voltage.
- The inductor L smooths the current, and R is the load.

**Conduction sequence.** The operation is the same in every interval; only the pair changes.

| Line voltage across the load | Thyristors conducting |
|---|---|
| $v_{AB}$ | T6, T1 |
| $v_{AC}$ | T1, T2 |
| $v_{BC}$ | T2, T3 |
| $v_{BA}$ | T3, T4 |
| $v_{CA}$ | T4, T5 |
| $v_{CB}$ | T5, T6 |

m">4π</text></svg><figcaption>Three-phase fully controlled bridge at α = 45° with continuous current. Each pair is fired α after its natural commutation point, so the output dips (and can go negative for α > 60°). V<sub>av</sub> = 1.35V<sub>LL</sub> cos α.</figcaption></figure>

- For $\alpha < 90°$ the average output is positive: the bridge works as a **rectifier**.
- For $\alpha > 90°$ (with a source such as a motor EMF in the load) the average is negative and it works as an **inverter**, sending power back to the AC supply.

## Output voltage

**Continuous current** (highly inductive load):

$$V_o = V_{av} = \frac{3\sqrt3V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha$$

where $V_m = \sqrt2V$ is the peak **phase** voltage. So

$$V_{av} = \frac{3\sqrt3(\sqrt2V)}{\pi}\cos\alpha = 2.34V\cos\alpha = 1.35V_{LL}\cos\alpha$$

**Purely resistive load.** For $\alpha \le 60°$ the output never reaches zero and the formula above still holds. For $\alpha > 60°$ the current becomes **discontinuous** and

$$V_o = \frac{3\sqrt3V_m}{\pi}\left[1 + \cos\left(\alpha + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] = 2.34V\left[1 + \cos\left(\alpha + \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right], \qquad 60° \le \alpha \le 120°$$

The rms output voltage for a resistive load ($\alpha \le 60°$) is

$$V_{rms} = \sqrt3V\left[1 + \frac{3\sqrt3}{2\pi}\cos2\alpha\right]^{1/2}$$

which gives $2.34V$ at $\alpha = 0$, as it must.

**Average current:** $I_{av} = V_{av}/R$; with a back EMF in the load, $I_{av} = (V_{av} - E)/R$.

## Currents and power factor, highly inductive load

With a ripple-free load current $I_o$:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Thyristor average current | $I_o/3$ |
| Thyristor rms current | $I_o/\sqrt3$ |
| rms input line current | $I_{L,rms} = \sqrt{2/3}\;I_o$ |
| rms fundamental line current | $I_{1,rms} = \dfrac{\sqrt6}{\pi}I_o = \sqrt3\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt2}{\pi}I_o$ |
| Fundamental apparent power | $S_1 = \sqrt3V_{LL}I_{1,rms} = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}$ |
| Real and reactive power | $P = P_1 = S_1\cos\alpha$, $\;Q = Q_1 = S_1\sin\alpha$ |
| Supply power factor | $pf = \dfrac{P}{\sqrt3V_{LL}I_{L,rms}} = \dfrac{3}{\pi}\cos\alpha$ |

## Worked example: 415 V, 100 A constant-current load

*The full-wave three-phase controlled rectifier has a three-phase 415 V, 50 Hz source (240 V phase) and provides a 100 A constant-current load. Determine (i) the average and rms thyristor current, (ii) the rms and fundamental line current, (iii) the apparent fundamental power $S_1$. If 25 kW is delivered to the DC load, calculate (iv) the supply power factor, (v) the DC output voltage, the load resistance and the delay angle, (vi) the real and reactive AC supply power, (vii) the delay-angle range if the AC supply varies by ±5% (with 25 kW and 100 A DC).*

1. $I_{Th,av} = 100/3 = 33.3$ A; $I_{Th,rms} = 100/\sqrt3 = 57.7$ A.
2. $I_{L,rms} = \sqrt{2/3} \times 100 = 81.6$ A; $I_{1,rms} = \dfrac{\sqrt6}{\pi} \times 100 = 78.0$ A.
3. $S_1 = \sqrt3 \times 415 \times 78.0 = 56.1$ kVA.
4. $pf = \dfrac{25\,000}{\sqrt3 \times 415 \times 81.6} = 0.426$.
5. $V_o = \dfrac{25\,000}{100} = 250$ V; $R_L = \dfrac{250}{100} = 2.5\ \Omega$. From $V_o = 2.34V_{ph}\cos\alpha$ with $V_{ph} = 415/\sqrt3$: $\alpha = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{250}{2.34 \times 239.6} = 63.5° = 1.11$ rad. (Check: $\frac{3}{\pi}\cos63.5° = 0.426$, the same power factor as in (iv).)
6. $P_1 = 56.1 \times \cos63.5° = 25$ kW; $Q_1 = 56.1 \times \sin63.5° = 50$ kVAr.
7. ±5% of 415 V is ±20.75 V.
   - At 394.25 V: $\alpha_1 = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{250}{2.34 \times 394.25/\sqrt3} = 62.0°$ (1.08 rad).
   - At 435.75 V: $\alpha_2 = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{250}{2.34 \times 435.75/\sqrt3} = 64.9°$ (1.13 rad).
   - So $62.0° \le \alpha \le 64.9°$.

> **Corrections to the class notes.** For a resistive load in discontinuous conduction the notes write $1 + \cos(\alpha + \pi/6)$; the bracket is $1 + \cos(\alpha + \pi/3)$, and it only applies for $\alpha > 60°$. The rms formula is written $(\sqrt3)(\sqrt2V)\sqrt{1 + \frac{3\sqrt3}{2\pi}\cos\alpha}$; the extra $\sqrt2$ must go and the angle is $2\alpha$, giving $\sqrt3V\sqrt{1 + \frac{3\sqrt3}{2\pi}\cos2\alpha}$ (otherwise $\alpha = 0$ would give $3.3V$ instead of $2.34V$). The example's lower delay angle, 61.9°, rounds to 62.0°.
